q: According to your notes, what did the 1966 White Paper do?

opts.t: It exposed high trauma death rates and started modern EMS
opts.why: Correct. The notes say: 1966 — White Paper exposed high trauma death rates and started modern EMS. The full title is not in the notes.

opts.t: It created NHTSA under the Department of Transportation
opts.why: Incorrect. NHTSA was created in 1970 under DOT. The 1966 White Paper exposed high trauma death rates and started modern EMS.

opts.t: It was the year AAOS published the first EMT textbook
opts.why: Incorrect. The first EMT textbook from AAOS is 1971. 1966 is the White Paper that exposed high trauma deaths and started modern EMS.

opts.t: It required every state to recognize EMR and AEMT
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes do not say that. 1966 is the White Paper on high trauma death rates that started modern EMS. Arizona historically recognized only EMT and Paramedic.

q: When was NHTSA created, and under which department, per your notes?

opts.t: 1970, under the Department of Transportation
opts.why: Correct. The notes: 1970 — NHTSA created under the Department of Transportation.

opts.t: 1966, under the Department of Health
opts.why: Incorrect. 1966 is the White Paper year. NHTSA was created in 1970 under the Department of Transportation. The notes do not place it under Health.

opts.t: 1971, under AAOS
opts.why: Incorrect. 1971 is when AAOS published the first EMT textbook. NHTSA was created in 1970 under DOT.

opts.t: 1970, as an independent medical board
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes say NHTSA was created in 1970 under the Department of Transportation, not as an independent medical board.

q: Who published the first EMT textbook, and in what year, according to the notes?

opts.t: AAOS in 1971
opts.why: Correct. The notes: 1971 — AAOS published the first EMT textbook.

opts.t: NHTSA in 1970
opts.why: Incorrect. 1970 is when NHTSA was created under DOT. The first EMT textbook was published by AAOS in 1971.

opts.t: The White Paper authors in 1966
opts.why: Incorrect. 1966 is the White Paper on trauma deaths. The first EMT textbook was AAOS in 1971. The White Paper’s full title/authors are not in the notes.

opts.t: The Medical Director in 1971
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes credit AAOS (1971) with the first EMT textbook, not a Medical Director.

q: How did EMS change as a system, per the notes?

opts.t: From pure transportation to a healthcare system with medical oversight
opts.why: Correct. The notes: EMS moved from pure transportation to a healthcare system with medical oversight.

opts.t: From hospital-based care to transportation only
opts.why: Incorrect. That is the opposite. The notes say EMS moved from pure transportation to a healthcare system with medical oversight.

opts.t: From paramedic-only crews to EMR-only crews
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes do not describe that shift. The system shift is transportation → healthcare with medical oversight.

opts.t: From online orders only to no medical director
opts.why: Incorrect. Every EMT and paramedic still works under a Medical Director. The shift is transportation → healthcare with medical oversight.

q: Match the level to the hours and role given in the notes.

opts.t: EMR ~50 hours, basic CPR and first aid; EMT ~130–150 hours, BLS foundation and limited meds
opts.why: Correct. Notes: EMR ~50 hours — basic CPR and first aid. EMT ~130–150 hours — BLS foundation, limited meds. AEMT hours are not given.

opts.t: EMT ~50 hours, basic CPR; EMR ~130–150 hours, BLS
opts.why: Incorrect. Those hours are swapped. EMR is ~50 hours (CPR/first aid). EMT is ~130–150 hours (BLS, limited meds).

opts.t: EMT ≥1,000 hours with 55–60 medications
opts.why: Incorrect. That is the paramedic line: ALS, ≥1,000 hours; advanced airways, EKG, 55–60 meds. EMT is ~130–150 hours, BLS, limited meds.

opts.t: AEMT ~50 hours and no IVs
opts.why: Incorrect. EMR is ~50 hours. AEMT is intermediate: IVs + expanded medications. Exact AEMT hours are not in the notes.

q: What do the notes say about the paramedic level?

opts.t: ALS, ≥1,000 hours; advanced airways, EKG, and 55–60 medications
opts.why: Correct. Notes: Paramedic — ALS, ≥1,000 hours; advanced airways, EKG, 55–60 meds.

opts.t: BLS foundation, ~130–150 hours, limited meds
opts.why: Incorrect. That is the EMT description. Paramedic is ALS, ≥1,000 hours, advanced airways, EKG, 55–60 meds.

opts.t: Intermediate IVs only, hours listed as ~50
opts.why: Incorrect. AEMT is intermediate (IVs + expanded meds; hours not given). EMR is ~50 hours. Paramedic is ALS ≥1,000 hours with advanced airways, EKG, 55–60 meds.

opts.t: Works independently without a Medical Director
opts.why: Incorrect. Every EMT and paramedic works under the Medical Director’s license. Paramedic training in the notes is ALS, ≥1,000 hours, advanced airways, EKG, 55–60 meds.

q: Who is legally responsible for the care an EMT or paramedic provides?

opts.t: The Medical Director — you work under that physician’s license
opts.why: Correct. Notes: every EMT and paramedic works under the license of a physician called the Medical Director, who is legally responsible for the care you provide.

opts.t: Only the EMT on scene; the physician is not involved
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes say the Medical Director is legally responsible and you work under that physician’s license.

opts.t: NHTSA, because it was created under DOT in 1970
opts.why: Incorrect. NHTSA’s 1970 creation is a history fact, not who is legally responsible for your care. That is the Medical Director.

opts.t: The receiving hospital’s charge nurse
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes name the Medical Director as legally responsible for the care you provide.

q: What do the Arizona notes say about recognized levels and jobs?

opts.t: Historically only EMT and Paramedic; EMR and AEMT were added recently, with limited job availability
opts.why: Correct. Notes: AZ historically recognized EMT and Paramedic only. EMR and AEMT were added recently, but job availability is limited.

opts.t: Arizona has always recognized EMR, EMT, AEMT, and paramedic equally
opts.why: Incorrect. Historically only EMT and Paramedic were recognized. EMR and AEMT were added recently, with limited jobs.

opts.t: EMR is the most common paid job in Arizona urban systems
opts.why: Incorrect. EMR/AEMT job availability is limited. Urban systems usually restrict advanced skills to paramedics.

opts.t: AEMT hours in Arizona are listed as 400 in the notes
opts.why: Incorrect. AEMT hours are not in the notes. AZ historically had EMT and Paramedic; EMR/AEMT were added recently with limited jobs.

q: Per the notes, who may start IVs in some rural Arizona agencies?

opts.t: Trained EMTs, with medical director approval
opts.why: Correct. Notes: some rural agencies allow trained EMTs to start IVs with medical director approval. Urban systems usually restrict advanced skills to paramedics.

opts.t: Any EMR, without approval
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes say some rural trained EMTs may start IVs with medical director approval — not EMRs without approval. Urban advanced skills are usually paramedic-only.

opts.t: Only the Medical Director in person on scene
opts.why: Incorrect. Rural trained EMTs may start IVs with medical director approval. The Medical Director does not have to be on scene for that approval.

opts.t: Urban EMTs as a standing statewide rule
opts.why: Incorrect. Urban systems usually restrict advanced skills to paramedics. Rural IV starts for trained EMTs require medical director approval.

q: Which care is listed as offline (standing orders) you follow without calling a doctor?

opts.t: CPR/AED, oxygen, and epinephrine for anaphylaxis
opts.why: Correct. Offline standing orders are pre-approved protocols for time-critical, standard care. Examples in the notes: CPR/AED, oxygen, epinephrine for anaphylaxis. Used for most routine emergencies.

opts.t: Certain pain medications, advanced procedures, and protocol deviations
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are the notes’ examples of when you need online (radio/phone) orders. Offline examples are CPR/AED, oxygen, and epi for anaphylaxis.

opts.t: Any new or unusual overdose antidote you invent on scene
opts.why: Incorrect. A rare overdose with the wrong antidote is the notes’ knowledge-based failure example. Unusual/unsure cases need online medical direction.

opts.t: Only care after you call and get a one-time order
opts.why: Incorrect. That describes online orders. Offline standing orders are pre-approved and followed without calling.

q: What is true of an online medical order, according to the notes?

opts.t: It applies to that one situation only — make another call for each new situation
opts.why: Correct. Notes: an online order applies to that one situation only — make another call for each new situation. Use when unsure, unusual, or you need extra authorization.

opts.t: Once given, you may reuse it all shift as a standing order
opts.why: Incorrect. Online orders apply to that one situation only. Standing orders are the offline, pre-approved protocols.

opts.t: It replaces the Medical Director for the rest of the patient’s hospital stay
opts.why: Incorrect. Online is real-time radio/phone direction for that one situation. You still work under the Medical Director’s license.

opts.t: You should call online before every routine oxygen or CPR call
opts.why: Incorrect. CPR/AED, oxygen, and epi for anaphylaxis are offline standing-order examples. Online is for outside protocol, certain pain meds, advanced procedures, deviations, or when unsure.

q: You know oxygen should be 15 LPM but you set the regulator to 2 LPM. Which error type is that?

opts.t: Skills-based failure (slip/lapse): you know the action but execute it wrong
opts.why: Correct. Notes: skills-based failure — you know the correct action but execute it wrong. Example given: set O2 to 2 LPM instead of 15 LPM.

opts.t: Rules-based failure: you applied a protocol to the wrong problem
opts.why: Incorrect. Rules-based is applying a known rule to the wrong situation (example: treat stroke as low blood sugar). Setting O2 to 2 instead of 15 LPM is the notes’ skills-based example.

opts.t: Knowledge-based failure: unfamiliar situation and a wrong plan
opts.why: Incorrect. Knowledge-based is a new/unfamiliar situation plus incomplete knowledge (example: rare overdose → wrong antidote). This is the skills-based O2 2 vs 15 LPM example.

opts.t: Secondary prevention failure
opts.why: Incorrect. Secondary prevention is early detection (screenings; early treatment of high blood pressure or cholesterol). This is a skills-based execution error.

q: Treating a stroke as low blood sugar is which error type in the notes?

opts.t: Rules-based failure — a known protocol applied to the wrong situation
opts.why: Correct. Notes: rules-based failure is applying a known rule/protocol that is wrong for this situation (misjudgment or misdiagnosis). Example: treat stroke as low blood sugar.

opts.t: Skills-based failure — you knew it was stroke but turned a dial wrong
opts.why: Incorrect. Skills-based is knowing the right action and executing it wrong (O2 2 vs 15 LPM). Treating stroke as low sugar is the rules-based example.

opts.t: Knowledge-based failure — rare overdose and the wrong antidote
opts.why: Incorrect. That is the notes’ knowledge-based example. Stroke treated as low blood sugar is rules-based.

opts.t: Primary prevention — stopping the problem before it starts
opts.why: Incorrect. Primary prevention examples are vaccines, seatbelts, and public education. This is a rules-based error.

q: A patient with decision-making capacity refuses transport after a partial leg amputation. What do the notes say?

opts.t: They can refuse treatment and transport; assess capacity carefully and document everything
opts.why: Correct. Notes: if the patient has decision-making capacity, they can refuse treatment and transport even if seriously injured (example: a partially amputated leg). Assess capacity carefully and document everything. If they later become unconscious or lose capacity, implied consent → treat and transport.

opts.t: You must transport anyway because the injury is too serious
opts.why: Incorrect. Capacity allows refusal even if seriously injured — the notes’ example is a partially amputated leg. Assess and document. Implied consent applies if they later lose capacity or become unconscious.

opts.t: Implied consent already applies because the injury is a true emergency
opts.why: Incorrect. Implied consent in Ch 1 is when they later become unconscious or lose capacity. With capacity they may refuse even a partial amputation.

opts.t: Honor a DNR only; refusal of transport is not allowed
opts.why: Incorrect. Advocacy includes honoring DNR/wishes, but consent is separate: capacity → may refuse treatment and transport. The amputation example is about refusal, not DNR.

q: What is the core personal-safety idea in the notes?

opts.t: Protect yourself first so you can help the patient — you cannot help anyone if you become a patient
opts.why: Correct. Notes: protect yourself first so you can help the patient. Includes scene safety, PPE, body substance isolation, safe lifting, and awareness. You cannot help anyone if you become a patient.

opts.t: Patient care comes before your own gloves or scene size-up
opts.why: Incorrect. Priority order is (1) your safety — gloves on every time (2) partner/crew (3) patient care. You cannot help if you become a patient.

opts.t: Only use PPE after the patient is loaded
opts.why: Incorrect. Personal safety includes PPE and BSI from the start. Protect yourself first.

opts.t: Situational awareness is optional if dispatch sounded calm
opts.why: Incorrect. Do a front-door survey, continuously scan, and re-check after tasks. Protect yourself first.

q: What is a front-door survey, per the notes?

opts.t: Before entering: look, listen, smell, and assess the mood
opts.why: Correct. Notes: do a quick front-door survey before entering — look, listen, smell, assess the mood. Then continuously scan the whole scene, not just the patient.

opts.t: After the call: restock and write the PCR only
opts.why: Incorrect. Front-door survey is before entering: look, listen, smell, assess the mood. End-of-shift cleaning/restock is a separate infection-control habit.

opts.t: Only check the patient’s pupils at the doorway
opts.why: Incorrect. The survey is look, listen, smell, and assess the mood — then scan the whole scene, not just the patient.

opts.t: Call hazmat for every doorway, even without fumes
opts.why: Incorrect. Hazmat is for chemical spills, unknown substances, strong chemical odors/fumes, toxic exposure, or industrial hazardous materials. The survey itself is look, listen, smell, mood.

q: When do the notes say to call police versus hazmat?

opts.t: Police: violence, weapons, threats, crime scenes, aggressive people, suspected abuse. Hazmat: spills, unknown substances, strong chemical fumes, toxic exposure, industrial hazardous materials
opts.why: Correct. That is the notes’ split for when to call for help.

opts.t: Police for chemical fumes; hazmat for suspected abuse
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are swapped. Police: violence, weapons, threats, crime, aggression, suspected abuse. Hazmat: chemicals, unknown substances, fumes, toxic exposure, industrial hazmat.

opts.t: Always call both before every medical call
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes list specific triggers, not a blanket both-every-time rule.

opts.t: Hazmat first for weapons; police only after patient care
opts.why: Incorrect. Weapons/violence → police. Do not enter an unsafe scene until it is made safe.

q: Which set is listed as fight-or-flight physical reactions?

opts.t: Faster HR and BP, faster breathing, dilated pupils, blood to muscles/heart/lungs/brain, slower digestion, tense muscles, more sweat, less pain, heightened senses
opts.why: Correct. The notes list those sympathetic + stress-hormone reactions. Hormone names beyond “stress hormones” are not in the notes.

opts.t: Slower HR, constricted pupils, blood pooled in the skin and gut
opts.why: Incorrect. Fight-or-flight increases HR/BP, dilates pupils, and redirects blood away from digestion and skin toward large muscles, heart, lungs, and brain.

opts.t: Only emotional numbness and nightmares during the call
opts.why: Incorrect. Nightmares, flashbacks, and emotional numbness are delayed stress signs (days/weeks/months later), not the immediate fight-or-flight list.

opts.t: Burnout, cynicism, and reduced performance in the first minute
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are cumulative stress signs from repeated calls over time, not the acute fight-or-flight body list.

q: Why do the notes say fight-or-flight matters on a call?

opts.t: Patient signs (fast HR, pale/cool/sweaty skin, nausea, anxiety) may be stress, not injury; it can look like shock; your own stress can impair decisions
opts.why: Correct. Notes: explains patient signs that may not be from injury; helps distinguish normal stress from true shock or critical illness; your own stress can impair decision-making.

opts.t: It proves the patient is in true shock and needs immediate blood products
opts.why: Incorrect. The point is it can look like shock but may be a normal stress response — you must distinguish them. Blood products are not in these notes.

opts.t: It only happens to EMTs, never to patients
opts.why: Incorrect. It is an automatic body reaction to perceived danger and is used to explain common patient signs as well as your own stress.

opts.t: It replaces the need to reassess the scene
opts.why: Incorrect. You still continuously reassess. Fight-or-flight explains signs and that your stress can impair decisions.

q: Match the EMS stress reaction to its timing and signs.

opts.t: Acute: during or right after (anxiety, fast HR, shaking, nausea, overwhelmed). Delayed: days/weeks/months (nightmares, flashbacks, irritability, numbness). Cumulative: repeated calls (burnout, fatigue, cynicism, reduced performance)
opts.why: Correct. That is the notes’ three-row table. Recognizing them helps prevent long-term issues like PTSD and burnout.

opts.t: Delayed happens only during the incident; acute happens years later
opts.why: Incorrect. Acute is during or right after. Delayed is days, weeks, or months later.

opts.t: Cumulative is a single call’s first 60 seconds only
opts.why: Incorrect. Cumulative builds from repeated stressful calls over time.

opts.t: All three are treated with a named defusing-team script spelled out in the notes
opts.why: Incorrect. Defusing-team procedures are flagged as not in the notes. The notes only define acute, delayed, and cumulative stress and that recognizing them helps prevent PTSD and burnout.

q: Pathogen, contamination, exposure, transmission — which matching is correct?

opts.t: Pathogen = disease-causing organism; contamination = it is on a person/object/surface; exposure = it contacts your body in a way that can infect; transmission = how it moves
opts.why: Correct. Examples in the notes: pathogen — HIV, MRSA, influenza (bacteria, virus, fungus, parasite). Contamination — blood on a stretcher, droplets on a doorknob. Exposure — needlestick, blood splash in the eye, inhaling droplets.

opts.t: Contamination means the pathogen has already infected you
opts.why: Incorrect. Infection after contact is the exposure idea. Contamination is the pathogen present on a person, object, or surface.

opts.t: Exposure means blood is only on the stretcher, not on you
opts.why: Incorrect. Blood on the stretcher is contamination. Exposure is when it enters or contacts your body in a way that can cause infection.

opts.t: A pathogen is only a chemical fume, not an organism
opts.why: Incorrect. A pathogen is a disease-causing organism (bacteria, virus, fungus, parasite).

q: Which transmission route do the notes pair with TB and measles?

opts.t: Airborne — tiny particles that stay in the air
opts.why: Correct. Notes: airborne — tiny particles that stay in the air (TB, measles). Droplet is large respiratory droplets, short distance. Vector-borne is mosquitoes/ticks.

opts.t: Droplet — large droplets, short distance only
opts.why: Incorrect. TB and measles are the airborne examples (tiny particles that stay in the air). Droplet is a different listed route.

opts.t: Vector-borne — mosquitoes and ticks
opts.why: Incorrect. That is the vector-borne definition. TB and measles are airborne examples.

opts.t: Indirect contact — touching a contaminated object only
opts.why: Incorrect. Indirect contact is touching a contaminated object. TB/measles are listed under airborne.

q: What is used every time under standard (universal) precautions?

opts.t: Hand hygiene and gloves for patient contact — assume every patient may be infectious
opts.why: Correct. Notes: assume every patient may be infectious. Used every time: hand hygiene; gloves for patient contact. Add eyes/mask/gown/N95 as needed.

opts.t: N95 on every medical call, even without airborne risk
opts.why: Incorrect. N95 is added for known or suspected airborne disease (must be fit-tested). Every-time items are hand hygiene and gloves.

opts.t: Gown and face shield as the minimum on every call
opts.why: Incorrect. Gowns when significant soiling is likely; eyes/face for splash, spray, or airway procedures. Minimum every time: hygiene + gloves.

opts.t: Mouth-to-mouth is preferred over a pocket mask
opts.why: Incorrect. Barrier devices (pocket mask or BVM with one-way valve) are always preferred over mouth-to-mouth.

q: When do the notes say to use soap and water instead of alcohol sanitizer?

opts.t: When hands are soiled, or after diarrhea cases (norovirus, C. diff). Sanitizer ≥60% if hands are not visibly dirty
opts.why: Correct. Hand hygiene: before and after every patient, after removing gloves, after touching contaminated items. Alcohol-based sanitizer (≥60%) when hands are not visibly dirty. Soap and water when soiled or after norovirus/C. diff.

opts.t: Sanitizer is required after C. diff; soap is only for clean hands
opts.why: Incorrect. Opposite. Soap and water after soiled hands or diarrhea cases (norovirus, C. diff). Sanitizer ≥60% when not visibly dirty.

opts.t: Never wash with soap once you have sanitizer on the truck
opts.why: Incorrect. Soap and water are required when soiled or after norovirus/C. diff.

opts.t: Use bleach on your skin if soap is not nearby
opts.why: Incorrect. After exposure, do not squeeze, suck, or apply bleach. Soap and water (or flush mucous membranes).

q: What is the donning (putting on) order in the notes?

opts.t: 1 hand hygiene 2 gown 3 mask/respirator 4 eye protection 5 gloves
opts.why: Correct. That is the listed donning sequence.

opts.t: 1 gloves 2 gown 3 eyes 4 mask 5 hygiene
opts.why: Incorrect. That is closer to doffing (gloves, gown, eyes, mask, then hygiene). Donning is hygiene, gown, mask, eyes, gloves.

opts.t: 1 mask 2 gloves 3 gown 4 hygiene 5 eyes
opts.why: Incorrect. Donning is hand hygiene → gown → mask/respirator → eye protection → gloves.

opts.t: Gloves first, then everything else in any order
opts.why: Incorrect. Gloves are last when donning so they go over the gown cuffs. Order: hygiene, gown, mask, eyes, gloves.

q: What is the doffing (taking off) order in the notes?

opts.t: 1 gloves 2 gown 3 eye protection 4 mask/respirator 5 hand hygiene
opts.why: Correct. That is the listed doffing sequence — dirtiest items first, mask last, then hygiene.

opts.t: 1 hygiene 2 gown 3 mask 4 eyes 5 gloves
opts.why: Incorrect. That is donning. Doffing is gloves → gown → eyes → mask → hand hygiene.

opts.t: 1 mask 2 gloves 3 gown 4 eyes 5 nothing
opts.why: Incorrect. Mask comes off after eyes, and hand hygiene is last. Order: gloves, gown, eyes, mask, hygiene.

opts.t: Pull the mask off first so you can breathe, then gloves
opts.why: Incorrect. Mask/respirator is step 4 of 5 (after gloves, gown, and eyes) so you do not contaminate your face; then hand hygiene.

q: Needlestick just happened. What is the immediate sequence in the notes?

opts.t: Turn care over to another EMS provider; wash with soap and water; do not squeeze, suck, or apply bleach; report immediately; seek evaluation ideally within hours
opts.why: Correct. Immediate: (1) hand off care (2) wash soap and water for needlestick/skin (3) flush eyes/mucous membranes with water or saline (4) do not squeeze, suck, or apply bleach. Then report immediately; medical evaluation right away (ideally within hours). PEP is most effective when started quickly; exact PEP drugs/hour windows are not in the notes. Evaluation/treatment at no cost to you.

opts.t: Finish the call first, then squeeze the wound and apply bleach
opts.why: Incorrect. Hand off care immediately. Do not squeeze, suck, or apply bleach. Wash with soap and water and report immediately.

opts.t: Force the source patient to give a new blood sample yourself
opts.why: Incorrect. You cannot force a new blood sample in most cases. Some states allow testing existing blood or testing under specific legal conditions.

opts.t: Wait until end of shift to tell anyone; PEP can start next week
opts.why: Incorrect. Report immediately; evaluate ideally within hours. Time matters — PEP is most effective when started quickly.

q: Parking and hazmat rules from the notes: which is correct?

opts.t: Park at least 100 feet from fires, crashes, and hazmat. First unit parks upstream (before the crash); later units downstream (past). Hazmat: uphill and upwind. NREMT: use the ERG
opts.why: Correct. Those are the numbered scene-safety facts in the notes.

opts.t: Park 10 feet away and downhill/downwind at hazmat
opts.why: Incorrect. Park at least 100 feet (or more for hazmat). Stay uphill and upwind.

opts.t: First unit parks past the crash (downstream) to leave room
opts.why: Incorrect. First on scene parks before the crash (upstream) to protect the scene. Second or later parks past (downstream).

opts.t: Enter the fire to locate the patient before fire personnel arrive
opts.why: Incorrect. Do not enter until fire personnel say it is safe. Stay clear of smoke and fire; watch collapse, explosion, toxic fumes.

q: Communicating with a critically injured patient — which matches the notes?

opts.t: Introduce yourself, orient them, be honest without being blunt or cruel, allow hope but not false hope, notify family as soon as practical
opts.why: Correct. Notes also: avoid appearing sad or grim; address initial refusal calmly. Example tone: “You’re seriously hurt, but we’re doing everything we can and getting you to the hospital quickly.” Do not completely recommend an option.

opts.t: Look grim, give false hope, and skip your name
opts.why: Incorrect. Avoid appearing sad or grim. Do not give false hope. Introduce yourself and explain what you are doing.

opts.t: Take away all hope so they understand how bad it is
opts.why: Incorrect. Allow for hope — do not take away all hope; do not give false hope.

opts.t: Wait to notify family until after hospital discharge
opts.why: Incorrect. Locate and notify family as soon as practical.

q: Kübler-Ross stages in the notes, and a key point about order?

opts.t: Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance — people may skip stages or move back and forth; they do not always go in order
opts.why: Correct. EMT role: respect and empathy; honest but compassionate; allow family with the patient when possible; avoid false hope or empty platitudes (“Everything will be fine”); support family even after care ends; stay professional.

opts.t: Acceptance, then denial only — always in that fixed order
opts.why: Incorrect. Listed order is denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance — and people do not always go through them in order.

opts.t: Bargaining is not one of the five stages in the notes
opts.why: Incorrect. Bargaining is stage 3 (“If I can just make it until…” or trying to make deals).

opts.t: Tell the family “Everything will be fine” as the required script
opts.why: Incorrect. Avoid false hope or empty platitudes (“Everything will be fine”).

q: When does a healthcare provider usually avoid legal exposure, per the notes?

opts.t: When they act in good faith and according to an appropriate standard of care
opts.why: Correct. Opening line of the notes: a healthcare provider usually avoids legal exposure if they act in good faith and according to an appropriate standard of care.

opts.t: Only if they never touch the patient
opts.why: Incorrect. The notes say good faith plus an appropriate standard of care — not refusing to treat.

opts.t: If they follow social media advice instead of protocols
opts.why: Incorrect. Standard of care is what a reasonably prudent EMT with similar training would do. Breaking confidentiality on social media can mean legal action, loss of certification, and termination.

opts.t: If they leave after a verbal goodbye with no handoff
opts.why: Incorrect. That risks abandonment (unilateral termination without consent and without transfer to equal or higher level). Legal protection is good faith + appropriate standard of care.

q: What is expressed consent in the notes?

opts.t: Alert, oriented, decision-making capacity; verbal or non-verbal agreement; must be informed (plan, risks, benefits)
opts.why: Correct. Example: ask to check BP and start an IV; patient says yes or holds out an arm.

opts.t: Unresponsive crash patient — treat without asking because a reasonable person would want care
opts.why: Incorrect. That is implied consent (unresponsive/severely altered, true emergency, reasonable-person assumption).

opts.t: A court order or mental health hold against the patient’s will
opts.why: Incorrect. That is involuntary consent.

opts.t: A living will alone that lists a ventilator preference
opts.why: Incorrect. A living will is an advanced directive. Expressed consent is an alert patient with capacity agreeing (verbal or non-verbal), and it must be informed.

q: How do informed consent and expressed consent relate in the notes?

opts.t: Informed is a more complete expressed consent (nature, risks, benefits, alternatives). All informed consent is expressed; not all expressed consent is fully informed
opts.why: Correct. Example of informed: explain risks of refusing transport for chest pain and they still agree to go.

opts.t: All expressed consent is fully informed, but informed consent is never expressed
opts.why: Incorrect. Opposite. All informed consent is expressed; not all expressed consent is fully informed.

opts.t: Informed consent is only for unresponsive patients
opts.why: Incorrect. Unresponsive patients fall under implied consent. Informed is a complete form of expressed consent.

opts.t: Informed consent replaces the need for capacity
opts.why: Incorrect. Expressed/informed require alert, oriented, decision-making capacity.

q: When do you use implied consent?

opts.t: Unresponsive, severely altered, or unable to consent; true emergencies only; assumes a reasonable person would want emergency care
opts.why: Correct. Example: unconscious crash patient — treat and transport. Key: lack of capacity + emergency → implied consent and treat.

opts.t: Any alert adult who says “yes” or holds out an arm
opts.why: Incorrect. That is expressed consent.

opts.t: Only after a signed living will is on the clipboard
opts.why: Incorrect. A living will alone is often not enough for EMS to withhold care. Implied consent is for patients who cannot consent in a true emergency.

opts.t: Whenever a family member on scene says to treat, even if the patient has capacity and refuses
opts.why: Incorrect. Capacity → can refuse. You may not share with family or treat on their say-so unless they are the legal decision-maker / have permission. Implied is for no capacity + emergency.

q: Which situation is involuntary consent in the notes?

opts.t: Suicidal, severely altered, refuses — law enforcement places a hold and you transport
opts.why: Correct. Involuntary: against the patient’s will under legal authority (mental health hold, court order, or lacks capacity and is a danger to self/others).

opts.t: Alert stroke-free adult with capacity refuses a bandage
opts.why: Incorrect. Capacity → they can refuse. Involuntary needs legal authority (hold, court, danger to self/others).

opts.t: Unconscious crash patient with no family present
opts.why: Incorrect. That is the implied-consent example (unresponsive, true emergency).

opts.t: Patient holds out an arm for a blood pressure cuff
opts.why: Incorrect. That is the expressed-consent example (non-verbal agreement).

q: If the patient has capacity, what may they refuse?

opts.t: Assessment, treatment, or transport — even if refusal may cause serious harm or death
opts.why: Correct. A competent adult with capacity may refuse even if refusal may result in serious harm or death. If they lack capacity and it is an emergency, treat under implied consent.

opts.t: Nothing — serious injury always forces transport
opts.why: Incorrect. Capacity allows refusal even if they may die. You explain risks, document, and cannot force treatment if they have capacity.

opts.t: Only transport, never assessment
opts.why: Incorrect. They may refuse assessment, treatment, or transport.

opts.t: They may refuse only after a POLST is signed on scene
opts.why: Incorrect. POLST/DNR is about withholding resuscitation if heart or breathing stops. Refusal is a capacity + informed + voluntary decision.

q: What four things should a patient be able to do when you assess capacity?

opts.t: Understand the information; appreciate the consequences; reason through the decision; communicate a clear choice
opts.why: Correct. Those are the four capacity bullets in the notes.

opts.t: Recite all 33 vertebrae and name every facial bone
opts.why: Incorrect. Capacity is understand, appreciate consequences, reason, and communicate a choice — not an anatomy quiz.

opts.t: Only say their name; no need to appreciate consequences
opts.why: Incorrect. Appreciating consequences is required, along with understanding, reasoning, and communicating a choice.

opts.t: Have a family member decide even though the patient is alert and capable
opts.why: Incorrect. If they have capacity, they decide. Family is not a substitute unless they are the legal decision-maker / have permission.

q: Which set is required for a valid refusal?

opts.t: Capacity; informed of condition, recommended care, and risks of refusing; voluntary; sign a refusal form when possible
opts.why: Correct. You must also explain risks, offer alternatives when appropriate, contact medical control for high-risk refusals, and document what you told them, responses, capacity, witnesses, and signature.

opts.t: Capacity is optional if they are angry
opts.why: Incorrect. Capacity is required for a valid refusal. Anger alone is not a substitute.

opts.t: You can skip explaining risks if they already look informed
opts.why: Incorrect. They must be informed of condition, recommended care, and risks of refusing.

opts.t: A coerced “yes” from a family member counts as the patient’s refusal
opts.why: Incorrect. Refusal must be voluntary (not forced or coerced) and from a patient with capacity (or the legal decision-maker).

q: Before leaving a refusal scene, what do the notes require?

opts.t: Reassess once more; confirm they still understand and are refusing; encourage calling 911 if worse; leave with a responsible person if possible; signed refusal or document refusal to sign; notify medical control if protocol requires
opts.why: Correct. That is the “before leaving” list.

opts.t: Leave immediately once they shake their head, with no recheck
opts.why: Incorrect. Reassess one final time and confirm they still understand and are refusing.

opts.t: Take them anyway if they will not sign
opts.why: Incorrect. If they have capacity you cannot force treatment. Get a signed refusal or document refusal to sign.

opts.t: Tell them never to call 911 again
opts.why: Incorrect. Encourage them to call 911 again if their condition worsens.

q: When is forcible/physical restraint allowed?

opts.t: Danger to self or others; needed to protect patient, crew, or public; needed to allow assessment/treatment; less restrictive options have failed
opts.why: Correct. Restraint is a last resort. Safety, monitoring, and documentation are critical.

opts.t: Whenever a patient is annoying or refuses a non-emergency bandage
opts.why: Incorrect. Allowed only for danger, protection, to allow care, and after less-restrictive options failed — last resort.

opts.t: To punish someone for yelling at the crew
opts.why: Incorrect. Not a listed reason. Least restrictive method; never for punishment.

opts.t: As the first step before talking to the patient
opts.why: Incorrect. Less restrictive options must have failed. Last resort.

q: Which restraint practices are forbidden or restricted in the notes?

opts.t: Never prone (face-down); never hog-tie; do not interfere with breathing or circulation
opts.why: Correct. Also: least restrictive method; consult medical control prior if possible; continuously monitor ABCs and mental status; document thoroughly; involve LE when possible.

opts.t: Prone and hog-tie are the preferred EMS methods
opts.why: Incorrect. Never prone; never hog-tie. Soft restraints (padded/Velcro) are preferred for EMS.

opts.t: You may ignore ABCs once straps are on
opts.why: Incorrect. Continuously monitor ABCs and mental status.

opts.t: Skip documentation if law enforcement is present
opts.why: Incorrect. Document thoroughly; involve LE when possible — both, not a trade.

q: Soft vs hard vs chemical restraint — what do the notes say?

opts.t: Soft (padded/Velcro) preferred for EMS; hard (handcuffs) usually LE only; chemical sedation is an ALS/paramedic skill, not normal EMT scope
opts.why: Correct. That is the types/chemical section.

opts.t: Handcuffs are the preferred EMT tool
opts.why: Incorrect. Hard restraints (handcuffs) are usually law enforcement only. Soft restraints are preferred for EMS.

opts.t: Chemical restraint is a routine EMT standing order in these notes
opts.why: Incorrect. Chemical restraint is an ALS/paramedic skill — not in normal EMT scope.

opts.t: Any provider may hog-tie if the patient is strong
opts.why: Incorrect. Never hog-tie. Use least restrictive; soft restraints preferred for EMS.

q: What patient information is protected, per the notes?

opts.t: Name, address, phone; history, findings, vitals; treatment and responses; anything that identifies the patient and their condition
opts.why: Correct. Share only with those who have a legitimate need to know for care, or when required by law. The chapter does not name a federal privacy statute.

opts.t: Only the patient’s name; vitals are public
opts.why: Incorrect. Vitals, findings, history, treatment, and anything that identifies the patient and their condition are protected.

opts.t: Nothing is protected once they call 911
opts.why: Incorrect. Information is private. If in doubt, do not share.

opts.t: Social media posts are fine if you omit the last name only
opts.why: Incorrect. You may not share on social media. Breaking confidentiality can mean legal action, loss of certification, and termination.

q: When may you share patient information?

opts.t: Care team (hospital, medical control, receiving facility); required by law (certain crimes, GSW, abuse, public health); valid court order/subpoena; patient’s written permission
opts.why: Correct. Those are the “may share” bullets.

opts.t: With the media if the story is newsworthy
opts.why: Incorrect. You may not share with the media.

opts.t: With friends or family automatically on every call
opts.why: Incorrect. Not with friends/family unless permission or they are the legal decision-maker.

opts.t: In casual talk with people not involved in care
opts.why: Incorrect. Casual conversation with people not in care is listed under “may not.”

q: A reporter asks what happened. What do the notes say?

opts.t: Do not share with the media. If in doubt, do not share
opts.why: Correct. May not: friends/family (unless permission or legal decision-maker), media, social media, casual talk. Breaking confidentiality can mean legal action, loss of certification, and termination.

opts.t: Give the name and vitals so the public is informed
opts.why: Incorrect. Name and vitals are protected. Media is a “may not share” example.

opts.t: Post a scene photo with the face cropped
opts.why: Incorrect. Social media is listed as not allowed.

opts.t: Tell bystanders the diagnosis because they already saw the ambulance
opts.why: Incorrect. Casual talk with people not involved in care is not allowed.

q: What is a living will / health care directive vs a DNR in the notes?

opts.t: Living will: which life-sustaining treatments they do or do not want (ventilator, feeding tube). DNR: no CPR/advanced resuscitation if heart or breathing stops
opts.why: Correct. Durable power of attorney names a proxy/agent. POLST/MOLST is a medical order with specific EMS/hospital instructions, often more detailed than a basic DNR.

opts.t: A living will is the same as a DNR and always stops EMS care
opts.why: Incorrect. A living will alone is often not enough for EMS to withhold emergency care — usually need a specific DNR or POLST.

opts.t: A DNR names a health-care proxy to make all decisions
opts.why: Incorrect. Naming a proxy is the durable power of attorney for health care. DNR is no CPR/advanced resuscitation if heart or breathing stops.

opts.t: POLST is only a diary of the patient’s feelings
opts.why: Incorrect. POLST/MOLST is a medical order with specific EMS/hospital instructions.

q: A living will is on the fridge but there is no DNR/POLST. The patient is in cardiac arrest. What do the notes say for EMS?

opts.t: A living will alone is often not enough to withhold emergency care — usually need a specific DNR or POLST. When in doubt, begin treatment and contact medical control
opts.why: Correct. Follow a valid DNR or POLST if present and appears legitimate. If any question, resuscitate and let the hospital sort it out.

opts.t: Always withhold CPR based on a living will alone
opts.why: Incorrect. Living will alone is often not enough for EMS to withhold. Usually need a specific DNR or POLST.

opts.t: Wait for the durable power of attorney to arrive before any care
opts.why: Incorrect. When in doubt, begin treatment and contact medical control. A POA names a proxy; it does not by itself tell you to wait.

opts.t: Tear up the living will; advanced directives never apply to EMS
opts.why: Incorrect. You must follow a valid DNR or POLST if present and legitimate. Living wills are weaker for EMS withholding decisions.

q: The patient is conscious and has capacity but there is a DNR in the chart. Whose wishes win?

opts.t: Current wishes override the written directive
opts.why: Correct. Notes: if conscious with capacity, current wishes override the written directive.

opts.t: The paper DNR always wins, even if they ask for care now
opts.why: Incorrect. Current wishes of a conscious patient with capacity override the written directive.

opts.t: The media’s request for an interview
opts.why: Incorrect. Media is not a decision-maker. Conscious + capacity → current wishes override the paper.

opts.t: A bystander’s opinion if they speak louder
opts.why: Incorrect. Capacity patient’s current wishes override the written directive — not a bystander.

q: Which are presumptive signs of death (not enough alone)?

opts.t: Unresponsiveness; no breathing; no pulse; fixed, dilated pupils
opts.why: Correct. Presumptive signs suggest death but are not enough by themselves to withhold resuscitation.

opts.t: Dependent lividity, rigor mortis, putrefaction, decapitation
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are definitive signs (obvious death — do not resuscitate).

opts.t: Only a signed living will with no DNR
opts.why: Incorrect. Living will alone is often not enough to withhold. Presumptive signs are unresponsiveness, apnea, pulselessness, fixed dilated pupils.

opts.t: Cynicism and burnout after many calls
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are cumulative stress signs from Chapter 2, not signs of death.

q: Which are definitive signs of death — obvious death, do not resuscitate?

opts.t: Dependent lividity; rigor mortis; putrefaction/decomposition; injuries incompatible with life (decapitation, massive trauma, etc.)
opts.why: Correct. Need a definitive sign or a valid DNR/POLST before withholding. When in doubt, start CPR.

opts.t: Unresponsiveness and no pulse only
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are presumptive and not enough alone.

opts.t: Fixed, dilated pupils by themselves
opts.why: Incorrect. That is a presumptive sign, not definitive.

opts.t: Anger at the crew during bargaining
opts.why: Incorrect. Anger/bargaining are grief stages (Ch 2), not definitive signs of death.

q: You find no pulse and no breathing, pupils fixed and dilated, but no definitive signs and no valid DNR/POLST. What do the notes say?

opts.t: Presumptive signs alone are not enough. When in doubt, start CPR
opts.why: Correct. You need a definitive sign or a valid DNR/POLST before withholding resuscitation. When in doubt, start CPR / begin treatment and contact medical control.

opts.t: Withhold CPR because four presumptive signs equal death
opts.why: Incorrect. Presumptive signs are not enough by themselves.

opts.t: Wait for the medical examiner before any CPR
opts.why: Incorrect. ME/coroner rules apply after death (don’t move the body until cleared). When in doubt on a possible salvageable patient, start CPR.

opts.t: Call the media before starting care
opts.why: Incorrect. Do not share with the media. When in doubt, start CPR.

q: When do you notify the medical examiner/coroner, and what is the first step?

opts.t: Unexpected death or previously good health; trauma, violence, accident, or suicide; suspicious/unusual; no recent attending physician. Notify law enforcement first. Do not move the body until ME/coroner clears it
opts.why: Correct. That is the ME/coroner section.

opts.t: Only after you move the body to the ambulance
opts.why: Incorrect. Do not move the body until the ME/coroner clears it. Notify law enforcement first.

opts.t: Every expected hospice death with a valid DNR, as the only trigger listed
opts.why: Incorrect. Listed triggers are unexpected/good health, trauma/violence/accident/suicide, suspicious, no recent attending physician.

opts.t: Call the reporter first so the scene is documented
opts.why: Incorrect. Notify law enforcement first. Do not share with the media.

q: What is the standard of care in the notes?

opts.t: What a reasonably prudent EMT with similar training and experience would do in the same or similar situation
opts.why: Correct. That is the definition given.

opts.t: Whatever the loudest family member demands
opts.why: Incorrect. Standard of care is the reasonably prudent EMT with similar training/experience in the same or similar situation.

opts.t: Whatever you saw once on social media
opts.why: Incorrect. Social media is not the standard — and posting about patients is forbidden.

opts.t: The maximum ALS skill, even if you are an EMT without that scope
opts.why: Incorrect. Avoid negligence by following protocols and staying in scope. Standard is similar training and experience.

q: Negligence requires which four elements — all of them?

opts.t: Duty to act; breach of duty; damages (harm); causation
opts.why: Correct. Failure to meet the standard of care that results in harm. All four required.

opts.t: Duty and breach only — harm is optional
opts.why: Incorrect. Damages (harm) and causation are also required. All four.

opts.t: Causation and a news story, without duty
opts.why: Incorrect. Duty to act is element 1. Media is irrelevant to the four elements.

opts.t: Abandonment plus a living will
opts.why: Incorrect. Abandonment is a separate concept. Negligence’s four elements are duty, breach, damages, causation.

q: What is abandonment?

opts.t: Unilateral termination of care without consent and without transfer to equal or higher level when the patient still needs care
opts.why: Correct. Avoid it: continuous care until proper handoff; never leave a patient who still requires care.

opts.t: A proper verbal handoff to a higher-level provider plus a completed PCR
opts.why: Incorrect. That is how you transfer care (also in Ch 4) — the opposite of abandonment.

opts.t: A valid informed refusal with capacity and a signature
opts.why: Incorrect. Documented informed refusal is how you avoid abandonment when they decline care.

opts.t: Waiting for police on an unsafe scene before entering
opts.why: Incorrect. If the scene is not safe, do not enter until made safe (Ch 2). Abandonment is leaving a patient who still needs care without consent or proper handoff.

q: How do you avoid both negligence and abandonment?

opts.t: Follow protocols and stay in scope; continuous care until proper handoff; document informed refusals; assess and document; never leave a patient who still requires care
opts.why: Correct. Key point: meet the standard of care, never leave a patient who still needs you, and document everything.

opts.t: Leave as soon as the ambulance doors close, PCR later if you remember
opts.why: Incorrect. Transfer is official only after verbal handoff to equal or higher plus a completed PCR (Ch 4). Never leave someone who still needs care.

opts.t: Try skills outside your scope if they seem helpful
opts.why: Incorrect. Stay within your scope and follow protocols.

opts.t: Skip the refusal form if they seem sure
opts.why: Incorrect. Obtain and document informed refusals when appropriate (signature or refusal to sign).

q: When in doubt about an advanced directive or possible death, what is the repeated rule?

opts.t: Begin treatment / start CPR and contact medical control; if any question, resuscitate and let the hospital sort it out
opts.why: Correct. Follow only a valid, present, applicable DNR/POLST. Presumptive signs are not enough. Doubt → treat.

opts.t: Withhold care until a living will is interpreted by the media
opts.why: Incorrect. Living will alone is often not enough; media must not get information. Doubt → resuscitate.

opts.t: Assume any unsigned note on the fridge is a valid DNR
opts.why: Incorrect. Follow a valid DNR or POLST if present and appears legitimate — not any scrap of paper.

opts.t: Wait for the ME before starting CPR on a pulseless patient with only presumptive signs
opts.why: Incorrect. Presumptive signs alone are not enough to withhold. When in doubt, start CPR.

q: A high-risk refusal is unfolding. Besides explaining risks, what should you do?

opts.t: Offer alternatives when appropriate, contact medical control for high-risk refusals, and document thoroughly (what you told them, responses, capacity, witnesses, signature)
opts.why: Correct. Valid refusal still needs capacity, informed, voluntary, and a signature when possible.

opts.t: Force them into the ambulance because the risk is high
opts.why: Incorrect. If they have capacity you cannot force treatment. Contact medical control for high-risk refusals.

opts.t: Ask the media to help persuade them
opts.why: Incorrect. Do not share with the media.

opts.t: Skip medical control because online orders are only for pain meds
opts.why: Incorrect. You must contact medical control for high-risk refusals (and Ch 1 says use online when unsure, unusual, or you need extra authorization).

q: For therapeutic communication, what order do the notes give for questions?

opts.t: Open-ended first (“What happened?”), then closed-ended for specifics
opts.why: Correct. Build trust and encourage the patient to share. Also: eye contact, speak clearly, listen actively, show respect. Adjust for age, culture, hearing/vision impairment, or anxiety.

opts.t: Closed-ended only, never let them tell the story
opts.why: Incorrect. Open-ended first, then closed-ended for specifics.

opts.t: Start with a leading question about chest pain
opts.why: Incorrect. Avoid leading questions (“The pain is in your chest, right?”). Open-ended first.

opts.t: Use medical jargon first to sound professional
opts.why: Incorrect. Avoid medical jargon (“You have tachycardia and dyspnea”). Use language they can understand.

q: “You said you don’t drink, but I smell alcohol.” Which type is that?

opts.t: Confrontation — point out an inconsistency calmly
opts.why: Correct. That is the notes’ confrontation example.

opts.t: Interpretation — restate what you think they mean
opts.why: Incorrect. Interpretation example: “It sounds like you’re worried this is a heart attack.” Confrontation points out an inconsistency.

opts.t: Explanation — tell them what is happening
opts.why: Incorrect. Explanation example: “I’m putting this oxygen mask on to help you breathe.”

opts.t: Summary — repeat main points
opts.why: Incorrect. Summary example: “Pain for two hours, started while walking, worse with deep breaths — correct?”

q: “It sounds like you’re worried this is a heart attack.” Which type?

opts.t: Interpretation — restate what you think they mean
opts.why: Correct. That is the notes’ interpretation example.

opts.t: Confrontation — inconsistency
opts.why: Incorrect. Confrontation is “You said you don’t drink, but I smell alcohol.”

opts.t: Explanation — what you are doing
opts.why: Incorrect. Explanation is “I’m putting this oxygen mask on to help you breathe.”

opts.t: Summary — recap the story
opts.why: Incorrect. Summary repeats main points back for confirmation.

q: “I’m putting this oxygen mask on to help you breathe.” Which type?

opts.t: Explanation — tell them what is happening
opts.why: Correct. That is the notes’ explanation example.

opts.t: Summary — repeat the history
opts.why: Incorrect. Summary is repeating main points of the story, not describing a treatment you are starting.

opts.t: Confrontation — point out inconsistency
opts.why: Incorrect. Confrontation is calmly pointing out a mismatch (alcohol example).

opts.t: False reassurance — a listed thing to avoid
opts.why: Incorrect. False reassurance is “Don’t worry, you’re going to be completely fine.” This line is the explanation example.

q: “Pain for two hours, started while walking, worse with deep breaths — correct?” Which type?

opts.t: Summary — briefly repeat the main points
opts.why: Correct. That is the notes’ summary example.

opts.t: Leading question — listed as something to avoid
opts.why: Incorrect. A leading question is “The pain is in your chest, right?” Summary confirms the story you already heard.

opts.t: Giving advice
opts.why: Incorrect. Giving advice example is “You should really quit smoking.”

opts.t: Judgmental statement
opts.why: Incorrect. Judgmental example is “Why did you wait so long to call us?”

q: Which of these is a listed thing to AVOID?

opts.t: False reassurance, leading questions, giving advice, interrupting, medical jargon, judgmental statements, talking over the patient with your partner
opts.why: Correct. Examples in the notes: “Don’t worry, you’re going to be completely fine”; “The pain is in your chest, right?”; “You should really quit smoking”; “You have tachycardia and dyspnea”; “Why did you wait so long to call us?”

opts.t: Open-ended questions like “What happened?”
opts.why: Incorrect. Open-ended first is recommended.

opts.t: Making eye contact and using the patient’s proper name
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are golden rules 1 and 2.

opts.t: Facing a hearing-impaired patient so they can read your lips
opts.why: Incorrect. That is golden rule 8.

q: Which set matches the 10 golden rules in the notes?

opts.t: Eye contact; your name and their proper name; tell the truth; language they understand; careful talk about them; body language; slow/clear/distinct; face hearing-impaired patients; time to answer; calm confident manner
opts.why: Correct. Those are the 10 golden rules for calming and reassuring patients.

opts.t: Talk over them with your partner and use jargon
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are listed as things to avoid, not golden rules.

opts.t: Give advice and leading questions first
opts.why: Incorrect. Avoid giving advice and leading questions.

opts.t: Say their full name over the radio as a courtesy
opts.why: Incorrect. Do not say the patient’s name over the radio. Golden rule 2 is provide your name and use their proper name when talking with them.

q: Radio and verbal reports — which is correct?

opts.t: Brief, clear, professional; plain English (avoid codes unless required); do not say the patient’s name over the radio; repeat orders back to confirm
opts.why: Correct. 10-codes and local radio templates are not in the notes.

opts.t: Always use 10-codes; the notes list them in full
opts.why: Incorrect. Use plain English (avoid codes unless required). 10-codes are flagged as not in the notes.

opts.t: Say the patient’s name twice so the hospital can chart it
opts.why: Incorrect. Do not say the patient’s name over the radio.

opts.t: Never repeat a physician order — just guess if you missed it
opts.why: Incorrect. Repeat orders back to confirm.

q: What does SBAR stand for in the notes’ hospital notification format?

opts.t: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation / ETA
opts.why: Correct. That is the format given. CHART/SOAP are noted as not the format given.

opts.t: Subjective, Breath sounds, Allergies, Rx
opts.why: Incorrect. SBAR is Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/ETA.

opts.t: Scene, Blood pressure, Airway, Response
opts.why: Incorrect. SBAR is Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation/ETA.

opts.t: SOAP only — SBAR is not in the notes
opts.why: Incorrect. SBAR is the format given. Full CHART/SOAP formats are flagged as not in the notes.

q: What must a PCR include, and what kind of document is it?

opts.t: Legal document / permanent medical record. Include demographics, chief complaint, history, vital signs, assessment findings, treatments, response to treatment, and times. Facts only
opts.why: Correct. Write objectively — no opinions or judgments. If it isn’t documented, it didn’t happen.

opts.t: An informal scratch pad you may throw away
opts.why: Incorrect. It is a legal document that becomes part of the permanent medical record.

opts.t: Opinions and judgments are preferred over facts
opts.why: Incorrect. Write objectively — facts only, no opinions or judgments.

opts.t: Treatments and times are optional
opts.why: Incorrect. Treatments, response to treatment, and times are required items.

q: “If it isn’t documented, it didn’t happen.” What does that go with?

opts.t: The PCR — accurate documentation protects the patient, protects you legally, and ensures continuity of care
opts.why: Correct. That phrase is in the PCR section. Key point of the chapter: clear communication and accurate documentation protect the patient, protect you legally, and ensure continuity of care.

opts.t: You may skip the PCR if the verbal handoff was friendly
opts.why: Incorrect. Leave a completed PCR. Transfer is official only after verbal handoff to equal or higher plus that PCR.

opts.t: Radio names replace written facts
opts.why: Incorrect. Do not say the name on the radio, and the PCR still must document the care.

opts.t: Only document if something went wrong
opts.why: Incorrect. Must include demographics, CC, history, vitals, findings, treatments, response, and times — the whole call.

q: When is transfer of care official?

opts.t: Only after a verbal handoff to a provider of equal or higher level, plus a clear oral report and a completed PCR
opts.why: Correct. That is the transfer-of-care section. Leaving without that is abandonment territory (Ch 3).

opts.t: When you park at the dock, even if no one takes report
opts.why: Incorrect. Official only after verbal handoff to equal or higher and a completed PCR.

opts.t: After you wave at a receptionist of lower training and leave
opts.why: Incorrect. Must be equal or higher level.

opts.t: The PCR can wait until next shift if you already spoke
opts.why: Incorrect. Leave a completed PCR with the oral report.

q: You made an error on the PCR. What do you do?

opts.t: Single line through the error, initial, date, write the correct information. Never erase or cover up
opts.why: Correct. That is the PCR-errors rule.

opts.t: Erase it completely so no one sees the mistake
opts.why: Incorrect. Never erase or cover up.

opts.t: Black out the line with marker
opts.why: Incorrect. Single line through, initial, date, write the correct information.

opts.t: Start a new PCR and shred the old one quietly
opts.why: Incorrect. Correct the error in place with a single line, initial, and date. It is a legal/permanent record.

q: Refusal documentation on the PCR must include what?

opts.t: Capacity, risks explained, patient understanding, and signature (or refusal to sign)
opts.why: Correct. Same theme as Ch 3’s refusal documentation. For children/special needs: speak at their level, involve caregivers, use simple language.

opts.t: Only the patient’s nickname
opts.why: Incorrect. Need capacity, risks explained, understanding, and signature or refusal to sign.

opts.t: A social-media summary for the family
opts.why: Incorrect. Protect all patient information. Share only with those involved in care or when required by law.

opts.t: Your opinion that they were “stupid to refuse”
opts.why: Incorrect. Facts only, no opinions or judgments.

q: What are the parts of a medical term in the notes?

opts.t: Prefix (beginning), word root (core meaning), combining vowel usually “o” (pronunciation only), suffix (ending)
opts.why: Correct. Break the word into prefix – root – suffix.

opts.t: Suffix first, then a combining vowel that changes the meaning
opts.why: Incorrect. The combining vowel is usually “o” for pronunciation only. Prefix beginning, root core, suffix ending.

opts.t: Only a root — prefixes and suffixes are not listed
opts.why: Incorrect. All four parts are listed: prefix, root, combining vowel, suffix.

opts.t: A number prefix is the only allowed part
opts.why: Incorrect. Numbers are special word parts, but terms still use prefix/root/suffix.

q: hyper- vs hypo- means?

opts.t: hyper- high/excessive; hypo- low/under
opts.why: Correct. Those are the listed speed/level prefixes.

opts.t: hyper- low; hypo- high
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are swapped.

opts.t: hyper- fast; hypo- slow
opts.why: Incorrect. Fast is tachy-; slow is brady-.

opts.t: hyper- without; hypo- after
opts.why: Incorrect. Without is a-/an-; after is post-.

q: tachy- vs brady- means?

opts.t: tachy- fast; brady- slow
opts.why: Correct. Listed prefixes.

opts.t: tachy- slow; brady- fast
opts.why: Incorrect. Swapped.

opts.t: tachy- high amount; brady- low amount
opts.why: Incorrect. High/excessive is hyper-; low/under is hypo-.

opts.t: tachy- before; brady- after
opts.why: Incorrect. Before is pre-; after is post-.

q: a-/an- and dys- mean?

opts.t: a-/an- without; dys- difficult/painful/abnormal
opts.why: Correct. Listed prefixes.

opts.t: a-/an- many; dys- none
opts.why: Incorrect. Many is multi-/poly-; none is nulli-.

opts.t: a-/an- around; dys- across
opts.why: Incorrect. Around is peri- or circum-; across/through is trans-.

opts.t: a-/an- same; dys- opposite
opts.why: Incorrect. Same is ipsi-; against/opposite is contra-.

q: pre- vs post- means?

opts.t: pre- before; post- after
opts.why: Correct. Listed prefixes. Ante- is also before/in front in the position list.

opts.t: pre- after; post- before
opts.why: Incorrect. Swapped.

opts.t: pre- under; post- above
opts.why: Incorrect. Under/below is sub-/infra-; above is supra-/super-.

opts.t: pre- within; post- outside
opts.why: Incorrect. Within is endo- or intra-; outside is ecto-/exo- or extra-.

q: Match the roots: cardi, hepat, nephr.

opts.t: cardi = heart; hepat = liver; nephr = kidney
opts.why: Correct. Only these roots appear in the notes — do not invent others.

opts.t: cardi = liver; hepat = kidney; nephr = heart
opts.why: Incorrect. cardi heart, hepat liver, nephr kidney.

opts.t: cardi = chest; hepat = mind; nephr = nerve
opts.why: Incorrect. Chest is thorac; mind is psych; nerve is neur.

opts.t: cardi = kidney; hepat = heart; nephr = liver
opts.why: Incorrect. cardi heart, hepat liver, nephr kidney.

q: Match the roots: neur, psych, thorac.

opts.t: neur = nerve; psych = mind; thorac = chest
opts.why: Correct. The six roots in the notes are cardi, hepat, nephr, neur, psych, thorac.

opts.t: neur = mind; psych = chest; thorac = nerve
opts.why: Incorrect. neur nerve, psych mind, thorac chest.

opts.t: neur = kidney; psych = liver; thorac = heart
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are nephr, hepat, cardi.

opts.t: neur = blue; psych = red; thorac = white
opts.why: Incorrect. Colors are cyan/o, erythr/o, leuk/o — not these roots.

q: Match: -itis, -pathy, -algia.

opts.t: -itis inflammation; -pathy disease; -algia pain
opts.why: Correct. Listed suffixes.

opts.t: -itis pain; -pathy removal; -algia inflammation
opts.why: Incorrect. Pain is -algia; removal is -ectomy; inflammation is -itis.

opts.t: -itis blood; -pathy breathing; -algia swallow
opts.why: Incorrect. Blood condition is -emia; breathing is -pnea; eating/swallowing is -phagia.

opts.t: -itis study of; -pathy enlargement; -algia abnormal condition
opts.why: Incorrect. Study of is -ology; enlargement is -megaly; abnormal condition is -osis.

q: Match: -ectomy, -megaly, -ology.

opts.t: -ectomy surgical removal; -megaly enlargement; -ology study of
opts.why: Correct. Listed suffixes.

opts.t: -ectomy enlargement; -megaly study of; -ology removal
opts.why: Incorrect. Rotated. -ectomy removal, -megaly enlargement, -ology study of.

opts.t: -ectomy inflammation; -megaly pain; -ology disease
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are -itis, -algia, -pathy.

opts.t: -ectomy breathing; -megaly blood; -ology swallow
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are -pnea, -emia, -phagia.

q: Match: -osis, -emia, -pnea, -phagia.

opts.t: -osis abnormal condition; -emia blood condition; -pnea breathing; -phagia eating/swallowing
opts.why: Correct. Listed suffixes.

opts.t: -osis removal; -emia study of; -pnea pain; -phagia heart
opts.why: Incorrect. Removal -ectomy; study of -ology; pain -algia; heart is the root cardi.

opts.t: -osis high; -emia low; -pnea fast; -phagia slow
opts.why: Incorrect. Those ideas are prefixes (hyper/hypo/tachy/brady), not these suffixes.

opts.t: -osis blue; -emia red; -pnea white; -phagia black
opts.why: Incorrect. Colors are cyan/o, erythr/o, leuk/o, melan/o.

q: Using only listed parts, tachycardia means?

opts.t: Fast + heart
opts.why: Correct. Study-guide build: tachycardia = tachy- (fast) + cardi (heart).

opts.t: Slow + breathing
opts.why: Incorrect. That is bradypnea (brady- + -pnea). Tachycardia is fast heart.

opts.t: Liver + inflammation
opts.why: Incorrect. That is hepatitis (hepat + -itis).

opts.t: Low + blood condition
opts.why: Incorrect. Hypo- + -emia is a low blood condition (study guide: hypoglycemia). Tachycardia is fast heart.

q: Using only listed parts, bradypnea means?

opts.t: Slow + breathing
opts.why: Correct. Study-guide build: bradypnea = brady- (slow) + -pnea (breathing).

opts.t: Fast + heart
opts.why: Incorrect. That is tachycardia.

opts.t: Without + eating/swallowing
opts.why: Incorrect. a-/an- + -phagia would be without eating/swallowing. Bradypnea is slow breathing.

opts.t: Difficult + heart
opts.why: Incorrect. dys- is difficult/painful/abnormal; cardi is heart. Bradypnea is slow breathing.

q: Using only listed parts, hepatitis means?

opts.t: Liver + inflammation
opts.why: Correct. Study-guide build: hepatitis = hepat (liver) + -itis (inflammation).

opts.t: Kidney + disease
opts.why: Incorrect. nephr + -pathy would be kidney disease. Hepatitis is liver inflammation.

opts.t: Nerve + pain
opts.why: Incorrect. neur + -algia would be nerve pain. Hepatitis is liver inflammation.

opts.t: Heart + enlargement
opts.why: Incorrect. cardi + -megaly would be heart enlargement. Hepatitis is liver inflammation.

q: Using only listed parts, hypoglycemia is explained as?

opts.t: Low + blood sugar condition (-emia = blood condition)
opts.why: Correct. Study guide: hypoglycemia = low + blood sugar condition (glycemia as blood condition is -emia).

opts.t: High + breathing
opts.why: Incorrect. High is hyper-; breathing is -pnea. Hypoglycemia is low + blood condition.

opts.t: Blue + abnormal condition
opts.why: Incorrect. That is cyanosis (cyan/o + -osis).

opts.t: Two + sides (not a blood condition)
opts.why: Incorrect. Bilateral = two sides (bi-). Hypoglycemia uses hypo- and -emia.

q: Using only listed parts, cyanosis means?

opts.t: Blue + abnormal condition
opts.why: Correct. Study-guide build: cyanosis = cyan/o (blue) + -osis (abnormal condition).

opts.t: White + blood condition
opts.why: Incorrect. leuk/o is white; -emia is blood condition. Cyanosis is blue + -osis.

opts.t: Red + inflammation
opts.why: Incorrect. erythr/o is red; -itis is inflammation.

opts.t: Gray + enlargement
opts.why: Incorrect. poli/o is gray; -megaly is enlargement.

q: bilateral, using listed parts, means?

opts.t: Two sides (bi- = two)
opts.why: Correct. Study-guide build: bilateral = two sides. bi- = two.

opts.t: One side (uni-)
opts.why: Incorrect. uni- = one. bi- = two.

opts.t: Four (quadri-)
opts.why: Incorrect. quadri- = four.

opts.t: None (nulli-)
opts.why: Incorrect. nulli- = none. bi- = two.

q: Match number prefixes: uni-, bi-, tri-, quadri-.

opts.t: uni- one; bi- two; tri- three; quadri- four
opts.why: Correct. Listed number parts.

opts.t: uni- four; bi- three; tri- two; quadri- one
opts.why: Incorrect. Reversed.

opts.t: uni- many; bi- none; tri- half; quadri- same
opts.why: Incorrect. Many is multi-/poly-; none is nulli-; half is hemi-/semi-; same is ipsi-.

opts.t: uni- around; bi- through; tri- behind; quadri- within
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are position parts (peri/circum, trans, retro, endo/intra).

q: Match: multi-/poly-, nulli-, hemi-/semi-.

opts.t: multi-/poly- many; nulli- none; hemi-/semi- half
opts.why: Correct. Listed number parts.

opts.t: multi-/poly- none; nulli- many; hemi-/semi- four
opts.why: Incorrect. multi-/poly- many; nulli- none; hemi-/semi- half; quadri- is four.

opts.t: multi-/poly- one; nulli- two; hemi-/semi- three
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are uni-, bi-, tri-.

opts.t: multi-/poly- yellow; nulli- black; hemi-/semi- gray
opts.why: Incorrect. Colors are cirrh/jaund/xanth yellow, melan/o black, poli/o gray.

q: Match colors: cyan/o, erythr/o, leuk/o.

opts.t: cyan/o blue; erythr/o red; leuk/o white
opts.why: Correct. Listed color parts.

opts.t: cyan/o red; erythr/o white; leuk/o blue
opts.why: Incorrect. cyan/o blue, erythr/o red, leuk/o white.

opts.t: cyan/o black; erythr/o gray; leuk/o yellow
opts.why: Incorrect. melan/o black; poli/o gray; cirrh/o, jaund/o, xanth/o yellow.

opts.t: cyan/o heart; erythr/o liver; leuk/o kidney
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are roots cardi, hepat, nephr.

q: Match colors: melan/o, poli/o, and the yellow group.

opts.t: melan/o black; poli/o gray; cirrh/o, jaund/o, and xanth/o yellow
opts.why: Correct. All three yellow combining forms are listed.

opts.t: melan/o white; poli/o blue; yellow is only leuk/o
opts.why: Incorrect. leuk/o is white; cyan/o is blue; yellow is cirrh/jaund/xanth. melan/o is black; poli/o is gray.

opts.t: melan/o gray; poli/o black; no yellow forms are listed
opts.why: Incorrect. Swapped black/gray, and yellow is listed three ways.

opts.t: melan/o red; poli/o yellow; cyan/o black
opts.why: Incorrect. Red is erythr/o; black is melan/o; gray is poli/o; yellow is cirrh/jaund/xanth.

q: ab- vs ad- means?

opts.t: ab- away from; ad- toward
opts.why: Correct. Same idea as movement: abduction away from midline; adduction toward midline.

opts.t: ab- toward; ad- away
opts.why: Incorrect. Swapped.

opts.t: ab- within; ad- outside
opts.why: Incorrect. Within is endo- or intra-; outside is ecto-/exo- or extra-.

opts.t: ab- same; ad- opposite
opts.why: Incorrect. ipsi- same; contra- against/opposite.

q: intra- vs inter-, and endo- vs ecto-/exo-?

opts.t: intra- within; inter- between; endo- within; ecto-/exo- outside
opts.why: Correct. extra- is also outside. The study guide flags these pairs to drill.

opts.t: intra- between; inter- within; endo- outside; ecto- within
opts.why: Incorrect. All swapped.

opts.t: intra- against; inter- same; endo- half; ecto- many
opts.why: Incorrect. contra- against; ipsi- same; hemi-/semi- half; multi-/poly- many.

opts.t: intra- before; inter- after; endo- above; ecto- below
opts.why: Incorrect. pre-/ante- before; post- after; supra-/super- above; sub-/infra- below.

q: ipsi- vs contra-, and peri- vs circum-?

opts.t: ipsi- same; contra- against/opposite; peri- around; circum- around (outside/full circle)
opts.why: Correct. Study guide highlights peri vs circum as both “around,” with circum specified as outside/full circle.

opts.t: ipsi- opposite; contra- same; peri- through; circum- behind
opts.why: Incorrect. ipsi- same; contra- opposite; trans- across/through; retro- behind/backward.

opts.t: ipsi- under; contra- upon; peri- beside; circum- within
opts.why: Incorrect. sub-/infra- under; epi- upon/on top; para- beside/near; endo-/intra- within.

opts.t: ipsi- one; contra- two; peri- three; circum- four
opts.why: Incorrect. Those are uni-, bi-, tri-, quadri-.

q: Directional terms — which matching is correct? (Always the patient’s right and left.)

opts.t: Superior = toward the head/above; inferior = toward the feet/below; anterior (ventral) = front; posterior (dorsal) = back
opts.why: Correct. Referenced to anatomical position: standing facing you, arms at sides, palms forward.

opts.t: Superior = feet; inferior = head; anterior = back; posterior = front
opts.why: Incorrect. All swapped.

opts.t: Anterior means the patient’s left only
opts.why: Incorrect. Anterior/ventral is the front. Right and left are always the patient’s, not yours.

opts.t: Dorsal is the front of the body
opts.why: Incorrect. Posterior (dorsal) = back; anterior (ventral) = front.

q: Medial, lateral, proximal, distal, superficial, deep — which is correct?

opts.t: Medial toward midline; lateral away; proximal closer to trunk/attachment; distal farther; superficial closer to surface; deep farther from surface
opts.why: Correct. Always on the patient’s body in anatomical position.

opts.t: Medial away from midline; distal closer to the trunk
opts.why: Incorrect. Medial is toward midline; distal is farther from trunk/attachment.

opts.t: Proximal means closer to the skin surface
opts.why: Incorrect. Closer to the surface is superficial. Proximal is closer to the trunk or point of attachment.

opts.t: Lateral means the patient’s midline
opts.why: Incorrect. Lateral is away from the midline.

q: Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction — which is correct?

opts.t: Flexion = bend / decrease angle (elbow or knee); extension = straighten / increase angle; abduction = away from midline (arm out); adduction = toward midline (arm back to side)
opts.why: Correct. Movement terms from the notes.

opts.t: Flexion straightens the joint; abduction is toward the midline
opts.why: Incorrect. Flexion bends/decreases the angle; abduction is away from midline.

opts.t: Adduction is arm circles; extension is toes down
opts.why: Incorrect. Arm circles are circumduction; toes down is plantar flexion.

opts.t: Abduction is palm up; flexion is head turning
opts.why: Incorrect. Palm up is supination; head left/right is rotation.

q: Supination, pronation, plantar flexion, dorsiflexion — which is correct?

opts.t: Supination = palm up; pronation = palm down; plantar flexion = toes down; dorsiflexion = toes up toward the shin
opts.why: Correct. Also in the notes: rotation = turn around an axis (head left/right); circumduction = circular (arm circles).

opts.t: Supination = palm down; dorsiflexion = toes down
opts.why: Incorrect. Supination is palm up; toes down is plantar flexion; dorsiflexion is toes up toward the shin.

opts.t: Pronation = toes up; plantar flexion = palm up
opts.why: Incorrect. Pronation is palm down; plantar flexion is toes down.

opts.t: These four terms are not in the notes
opts.why: Incorrect. All four are listed under movement.

q: Patient positions — which matching is correct?

opts.t: Supine: back, face up. Prone: stomach, face down. Lateral recumbent (recovery): on the side. Fowler: sitting upright ~45–90°. Semi-Fowler: ~30–45°
opts.why: Correct. Document the position clearly (“found supine,” “transported semi-Fowler”). Anatomical position: standing upright, facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward.

opts.t: Supine is face down; prone is face up
opts.why: Incorrect. Supine is back/face up; prone is stomach/face down.

opts.t: Fowler is 30–45° and semi-Fowler is 45–90°
opts.why: Incorrect. Those degree ranges are swapped. Fowler ~45–90°; semi-Fowler ~30–45°.

opts.t: Recovery position is Trendelenburg (feet higher than head)
opts.why: Incorrect. Recovery is lateral recumbent (on the side). Trendelenburg is supine, feet higher than head (rarely used now). Shock position is supine with legs elevated (older term; use caution).

q: Anatomy vs physiology vs topographic anatomy?

opts.t: Anatomy = structure (what it looks like and where); physiology = function (how it works); topographic = external landmarks/surface features used to locate deeper structures
opts.why: Correct. Always referenced to anatomical position: standing upright, facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward. Learn directional terms and surface landmarks first. Later body systems after the skeleton are not in these notes.

opts.t: Anatomy is function; physiology is only surface landmarks
opts.why: Incorrect. Anatomy is structure; physiology is function; topographic anatomy is surface landmarks.

opts.t: Topographic anatomy means listing skull bones beyond the four named in the notes
opts.why: Incorrect. Extra skull bones beyond the listed four are flagged as not in the notes. Cranium in the notes is 4 bones: frontal, parietal (2), occipital. Topographic anatomy is external landmarks/surface features.

opts.t: Physiology is the 206-bone count only
opts.why: Incorrect. 206 is an anatomy fact about the adult skeleton. Physiology is function.

q: Anatomical position in these notes is?

opts.t: Standing upright, facing forward, arms at sides, palms facing forward
opts.why: Correct. Topographic anatomy and directional terms are always referenced to that position.

opts.t: Prone, palms down, facing the stretcher
opts.why: Incorrect. Prone is a patient position (stomach, face down) from Ch 5. Anatomical position is standing, face forward, arms at sides, palms forward.

opts.t: Semi-Fowler at 30–45°
opts.why: Incorrect. That is a transport/found position (Ch 5), not the reference anatomical position.

opts.t: Supine with feet higher than the head
opts.why: Incorrect. That is Trendelenburg (rarely used now).

q: The sagittal and midsagittal planes divide the body how?

opts.t: Sagittal: left and right. Midsagittal (median): equal left and right halves
opts.why: Correct. Notes: sagittal divides left and right; midsagittal (median) = equal halves.

opts.t: Sagittal: front and back
opts.why: Incorrect. Front and back is coronal (frontal).

opts.t: Sagittal: upper and lower (cross-section)
opts.why: Incorrect. That is transverse (horizontal/axial).

opts.t: Midsagittal means unequal left/right slices
opts.why: Incorrect. Midsagittal is equal halves.

q: Coronal (frontal) vs transverse (horizontal/axial)?

opts.t: Coronal: front (anterior) and back (posterior). Transverse: upper (superior) and lower (inferior); also called a cross-section
opts.why: Correct. Those are the other two planes in the notes.

opts.t: Coronal: left and right; transverse: front and back
